<h2>Personal Reflections on Exercising and Activeness</h2>

<p>I&#39;ve started having a tough time about framing why I move and hope to understand it some more to focus my objectives. I want to spend a little time here to journal a breakdown and see what comes of it on the other end.</p>
<p>Don&#39;t get me wrong, it&#39;s still lots of fun but it&#39;s getting difficulty contextualizing these experiences, which are all so incredible, but starting to blur in terms of excitedness. Perhaps its that it has become less goal oriented and more experience driven.</p>

<p>In the past when I was focused more on running and rugby the kinds of goals you had were:<br>- Stick to __x__ pace to achieve a sub 1hr45min half marathon,<br>- Win __x__ tournament by becoming a more explosive, accurate passing, pitch intelligent half-back in Rugby 7s<br>These goals are measurable and comparable between efforts. And with that, training became more intentional.</p>
<p>Nowadays, I don&#39;t sign up for races, nor do I have plans to, and I&#39;m not trying to push certain personal time goals in specific disciplines, which are honestly goals I&#39;ve not been interested in pursuing. There have been also been many joys of being more experience driven. Unfortunately, being experience driven is becoming a more abstract concept for me understand I am beginning to feel dissatisfied that I don&#39;t have a good way to value it - perhaps I need to put goals for future experiences. The dissatisfaction stems from some questions of these questions:<br>1. What is a good/satisfying experience?<br>2. Why pursue those experiences?<br>3. How do we sustainably and continuously enjoy experiences?</p>
<p>We&#39;ll start with these 3 questions</p>

<p>Q1. What is a good/satisfying experience?</p>
<p>Below are what I&#39;ve noticed are patterns of what missions I gravitate towards.</p>
<p>- There&#39;s something new and obscure about the mission - a place I haven&#39;t been to, a type of route I haven&#39;t experienced. There&#39;s something incredibly gratifying about seeing and experiencing something that you had to work for, put time into, hurt and struggle for.</p>
<p>- The idea of the has to mission emotionally excite me, typically because the mission straddles the line of being an interesting idea and, on the other side, being outlandish and a little stupid if I&#39;m being honest,</p>
<p>- I want to be challenged physically - Something weird happened to me on Mt.Whitney for which I flew out for to do, had planned for months in advance, and where I was having a great time while being there, but I came down that mountain feeling dissatisfied because I had honestly had too relaxed of a time out there (I am also aware that I sound like a twat admitting this). I had hoped for a multi-day sufferfest and it ended up being a physically relaxed time. I guess I hate relaxation or my idea of relaxation is pretty fucked up. Just to be clear, I will never take that experience for granted. I also got to spend the weekend with one of my best friends so it was always going to be a fantastic time.</p>
<p>- Having time for personal thought and reflection - I love doing missions with friends. It is so beautiful to be able to share them with others. But, I have had a few incredible experiences where I&#39;ve done missions on my own, or have had chunks of time on my own, and in those moments it has allowed me to enter deep thought, meditative thought, or connect with a spiritual side of me that I didn&#39;t know really existed. Some of the moments when these types of thoughts have occurred have become highlights of entire missions (longs peak comes to mind and feeling Connor&#39;s presence).</p>

<p>Q2. Why pursue those experiences?</p>
<p>Mountaineers and climbers, when asked why they summit mountains and climb crazy faces, always answer that it is &quot;because we can.&quot; I call bullshit, it feels like a copout answer. There&#39;s just gotta something deeper driving this. The need to feel accomplishment, acceptance, respect, or maybe the combo and more? </p>
<p>Some objectives I&#39;ve done are easy to define. For example, climbing and skiing Mt.Shasta, that was an epic mission (18hrs, 7ft vert, highly technical) that is obvious why it was epic. Longs Peak, a well known local 14er with a reputation for being hard. I surprised myself with completing it in half the time it takes most people and felt comfortable doing it solo even with the mild technical challenges involved. But some aren&#39;t so easy to define why they were good. The Bolinas weekend as the last weekend in California. That was wrapped up in community, nostalgia, a variety of planned and spontaneous events. </p>
<p>So what is the why? I&#39;m actually still not sure. Is it to create lasting memories? To prove that I can do something? To show off or impress and to who? Peers? Myself? These missions are all inherently selfish pursuits. </p>
<p>What I do know is that I gain huge satisfaction from these missions. They give me belief that I can do more, that I can do harder things and more profound things. It&#39;s a discussion that Alex and I and the conclusion we came to too. They also allow me to move into my day-to-day with purpose and resolve. It makes me want to keep training, moving, being prepared, and in turn it helps my physical and mental health. It makes me want to work hard at my professional and educational pursuits so that goals are achieved in those realms to justify these fun pursuits.</p>

<p>Q3. How do we sustainably and continuously enjoy experiences?</p>
<p>Physically. I&#39;m now in a place where I feel blessed to have the fitness and breadth of knowledge to tackle many objectives and for them to feel within limits before the outdoors objectives become too niche and really silly (although Mummy Mania feels quite silly). I&#39;ve been rotating between cycling, swimming, and running ~5days a week, getting 3-4 lifts in a week, and doing weekend missions. I&#39;ve spent time focusing on functional strength for injury prevention when doing cardio with legs and have become fairly disciplined with diet. It&#39;s all been quite sustainable and I love that. But think I need to be more reflective when I exercise to identify and anticipate problems to solve. Like recently, I pulled my upper glute running - I know it&#39;s because I&#39;ve been slacking on glute work in the gym (cause it sucks to do), but I should be more aware and always asking where the next injury could come from.</p>
<p>Mentally. This thought process on the what and why of pursuing an experience hopefully helps me to appreciate it more in the moment. I like that there is still a hunt for the ridiculous, a little showing off, the stoke of undertaking a big challenge. But now I need to truly accept that I love these aspects so that I can remember that as I am doing it, not only in the before and after.</p>

<p>I&#39;m now in a place where I feel blessed to have the fitness and breadth of knowledge to tackle many objectives and for them to feel within limits before the outdoors objectives become too niche and really silly (although Mummy Mania feels quite silly). I&#39;ve been rotating between cycling, swimming, and running ~5days a week, getting 3-4 lifts in a week, and doing weekend missions. I&#39;ve spent time focusing on functional strength for injury prevention when doing cardio with legs and have become fairly disciplined with diet. It&#39;s all been quite sustainable and I love that. But it&#39;s unfocused. It leaves me with questions like:<br>* What am I training for?<br>* How well am I actually performing?<br>* Am I optimizing how I&#39;m performing?<br>* How do I actually improve as a athlete?<br>* What does it even mean to be a better athlete if I don&#39;t have discrete ways to measure improvement?</p>

<p>I shouldn&#39;t forget that I also do this for the people who can&#39;t. This is a way I can honour them and bring them with me spiritually. Be reminded that time and life is precious. It&#39;s a blessing to exist and sometimes you get to share it with people. Some friends and peers have even started getting back into shape or picked up running because they said I inspired them to do so. It&#39;s pretty amazing. I guess just by being is an okay way to give back. It&#39;s okay. Remind yourself that it&#39;s okay.</p>

<p>Warren Buffet talks about keeping an inner-scorecard with your own measures and guidelines for success, as opposed to an outer-scorecard, which is guided by external validation and status. But, maybe you can have both. Maybe they allow the other to score higher. Building community by doing your own thing and gaining admiration when that occurs makes me reflect more and refine my inner-scorecard. Maybe it&#39;s not so bad of a thing.</p>

<p>I could write a conclusion I guess. But I&#39;ve never been good at those. I like to let the work speak for itself and open for interpretation. God, why am I so existential about everything. It&#39;s also okay to just let things be what they are and not think about them so much (aka retard-max)</p>
<p>But I will say that that was very cathartic but at the same time exposing. I&#39;m kind of a self-indulging cunt in how I think. But I also find deep pleasure and importance of building community, helping my friends, being kind, and to give love. So if you have a problem with that, suck it - you&#39;re probably a chud hahaha. </p>
